title: Non-Examples: How Showing What Something ISN'T Sharpens What IT IS
author: Jamie Clark
summary: Jamie Clark provides a comprehensive, evidence-grounded guide to non-examples—deliberately chosen contrast cases that share surface features with a concept but lack its critical defining feature—arguing they are essential tools for forming accurate conceptual schema rather than optional additions to teaching. Drawing on Archer and Hughes' Explicit Instruction (2011), Engelmann and Carnine (1982), and Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, Clark explains that examples alone create either too-narrow or too-broad schema; non-examples define the boundary between what something is and what it is not. The piece systematically distinguishes non-examples from random wrong answers, trick questions, and misconceptions, and provides a five-step implementation framework: identify the critical feature, choose non-examples that share surface features, sequence examples and non-examples consecutively, include boundary examples, and use pause-and-reflect routines. The pathetic fallacy illustration—showing how students who learn pathetic fallacy from examples alone begin labeling every weather reference as pathetic fallacy—demonstrates the real cost of omitting non-examples from instruction.
points: Identify the single critical defining feature of a concept before choosing any examples or non-examples—if you cannot name it clearly, your students cannot either.
Design non-examples that share surface features with examples but differ only in the critical feature; non-examples that are too obviously wrong teach nothing and create no productive cognitive work.
Sequence examples and non-examples consecutively so students compare in real time rather than from memory—the consecutive pairing is what makes the critical feature visible.
Include boundary examples that sit right at the conceptual edge to stretch understanding beyond obvious cases; this is where genuine conceptual understanding gets tested.
Use the pause-and-reflect routine after each example/non-example pair before revealing the answer—the ten-second pause is not dead time but the moment cognitive work happens.
quotes: Learning is driven by clear distinctions — knowing what something is requires knowing what it isn't.
In order to establish the boundaries of when and when not to apply a skill, strategy, concept, or rule, provide a wide range of examples and non-examples.
I am a huge believer that in order to really understand something we must know both what it is and what it is not, hence I love a non-example.
Non-examples don't add complexity to a lesson. They remove the ambiguity that causes problems later.
A misconception formed in Year 7 doesn't sit quietly — it actively interferes with everything built on top of it.
